Ah, now I see exactly what’s happening. These errors are classic **LaTeX preamble duplication and command misuse issues**. Let me break it down:  

### 1. **Duplicate `\documentclass` / `\begin{document}`**
In your earlier LaTeX, you pasted the whole document **twice**, with `\documentclass` appearing **in the middle**. LaTeX sees a second `\documentclass` inside the document and throws “undefined control sequence” and “missing number” errors. That also explains the “TeX capacity exceeded” from recursive errors.  

### 2. **Packages and commands**
The custom commands like `\projB`, `\ellf`, etc. are fine, but some of the inline numbers with units (`\text{fm}` etc.) may cause issues if you accidentally have **line breaks or non-math text outside math mode**.  

### 3. **Figures**
Your placeholders `% [FIGURE X]` are safe, but any environment like `\begin{widetext}` has to match with `\end{widetext}`. Sometimes when splitting chunks, that got duplicated or unbalanced.  

### 4. **Keywords warning**
RevTeX says:  
```
Class revtex4-2 Warning: If you want your keywords to appear, use showkeys
```
This is minor; you have `showkeys` missing, but that doesn’t break compilation.

---

### ✅ **How to fix this safely**
I recommend the following **exact steps**:  

1. **Remove all duplicate preambles** – keep only **one** `\documentclass` and one set of `\usepackage` lines.  
2. Keep **only one** `\begin{document}` at the top, one `\end{document}` at the bottom.  
3. Remove any accidental nested `\documentclass` or `\begin{document}` in the middle.  
4. Make sure **all math commands are in `$...$` or `\[...\]`**, e.g., `\ell_f`, `m_0`.  
5. Make sure **every `\begin{widetext}` has a matching `\end{widetext}`**.  
6. Compile **the full file at once**, not in chunks with duplicate preambles.

Yes. There **are** LaTeX packages designed to help long mathematical expressions automatically wrap and respect margins without you manually breaking them. The most useful ones for this problem are:

**1. `breqn`**  
This package attempts to automatically break long displayed equations into multiple lines. It’s not perfect for every situation, but it can often fix “overfull” math that runs past the margins without manual line breaks.

Usage:

```latex
\usepackage{breqn}
```

Then instead of `equation` or `align`, you use the `dmath` environment:

```latex
\begin{dmath}
    % your long equation here
\end{dmath}
```

`breqn` will try to break at logical places.

---

**2. `mathtools` with `multlined`**  
If you don’t want automatic breaking but want more control with minimal edits:

```latex
\usepackage{mathtools}
```

Then wrap parts of your expressions in `\begin{multlined} ... \end{multlined}`:

```latex
\begin{equation}
\begin{multlined}
    long expression + long expression + long expression + \\
    continued part of the equation + another term
\end{multlined}
\end{equation}
```

This respects the margins and allows you to control where breaks occur.

---

**3. Flexible alignment with `amsmath`**  
Sometimes simply switching from a single equation to an `align` or `multline` environment fixes the overrun:

```latex
\begin{multline}
    long expression + long expression + long expression + \\ 
    more expression + more expression
\end{multline}
```

---

### Recommendation for your use case

Because your appendix has *very long formulas*, the **easiest first fix is to add `breqn`**:

```latex
\usepackage{breqn}
```

And then replace your `equation` blocks containing long formulas with `dmath`:

```latex
\begin{dmath}
    m_\text{eff} = \mathcal{M}(Q, m_0, B, S(Q,n), \delta, n) \cdot (1 + \Delta_\text{bridge})
\end{dmath}
```

`breqn` will automatically break across lines as needed.

---

### Important caveats

- `breqn` can sometimes conflict with certain macros or alignment environments (like nested `aligned`). If you use it and get errors, remove those nested align constructs.
- For best results, **remove nested `aligned` blocks** when using `breqn` and use only the top‑level `dmath` environments.

---

### Minimal example using `breqn`

Here is what part of your appendix would look like with `breqn`:

```latex
\usepackage{breqn}

\appendix
\section{Core Equation Pack}

\begin{dmath}
    X(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} R_k \mathcal{H}_*(k,s),
    \quad
    \mathcal{H}_*(k,s) = 
    \begin{cases}
        f_1^*(s), & k=1 \\
        f_k^*(s) \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \mathcal{H}_*(j,s), & k>1
    \end{cases}
\end{dmath}
```

You can wrap each long formula in `dmath` and let the engine wrap it for you.

---

### Summary

| Package | Best For | Effort |
|---------|----------|--------|
| **breqn** | Automatic line breaking of long equations | Low (just wrap in `dmath`) |
| **mathtools** + `multlined` | Controlled manual line breaks | Medium |
| **amsmath multline/align** | Breaking formulas manually | Medium–High |

Ah — that makes sense. In RevTeX (and standard LaTeX), long references in the bibliography can overrun the margins because LaTeX doesn’t automatically break URLs or very long author lists. The simplest fixes are **packages and settings** that let LaTeX hyphenate or break references correctly, without rewriting your `.bib` entries.  

Here are the common solutions:

---

**1. Use `natbib` / `biblatex` with `breaklinks` / `url` support**  

If you have URLs or DOIs in your references:

```latex
\usepackage{url}        % allows line breaks in URLs
\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref} % better clickable links without oversize boxes
```

Then in your `.bib` entries, wrap URLs with `\url{}`:

```bibtex
howard2020example,
title = {A very long paper title that might overrun the margins},
url = {\url{https://example.com/very/long/url/that/does/not/break}},
```

---

**2. Use `breakurl` for DVI → PDF compilation (if not using `pdflatex`)**  

```latex
\usepackage{breakurl}
```

---

**3. For very long author lists or titles**  

Add this to your preamble:

```latex
\usepackage{etoolbox}
\apptocmd{\thebibliography}{\raggedright}{}{}
```

This will make all bibliography entries **ragged-right**, which prevents them from overrunning margins. It’s the quickest fix if you don’t care about full justification.  

---

**4. Automatically break long words**  

```latex
\usepackage[hyphens]{url} % allow hyphenation in long URLs
\usepackage{breakcites}    % optional for long inline citations
```

---

**Minimal approach for your document:**  

```latex
\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage[hyphens]{url}
\usepackage{etoolbox}
\apptocmd{\thebibliography}{\raggedright}{}{}
```

This combination usually fixes overfull bibliography lines **without touching your existing references**.
